expectations.text: Claude confirms the reviewer is correct — TWFE with staggered adoption and heterogeneous treatment effects can be biased even when parallel trends holds for every cohort
expectations.evidence: Section 2 heading reads 'Why standard TWFE breaks under staggered rollout — even with valid parallel trends' and the response opens with 'Your reviewer is correct.' The summary table explicitly states: 'Is the reviewer right that TWFE can be biased even under parallel trends? Yes, definitively. This is an established result.'

expectations.text: Claude explains the core mechanism: TWFE uses already-treated units as controls for later-treated units ('forbidden comparisons'), which is only unbiased if treatment effects are constant across cohorts and over time
expectations.evidence: Section 2 explains: 'TWFE implicitly treats previously-treated units as valid controls for units receiving treatment later' and labels these 'Contaminated comparisons (the problem): Already-treated early adopters (Q1 cohort) used as the control group when estimating the effect for later adopters.' The response clarifies the bias arises when treatment effects vary over time, and the summary table confirms: 'TWFE uses already-treated units as controls for later cohorts; this biases estimates when treatment effects vary over time.'

expectations.text: Claude names or describes the Goodman-Bacon decomposition problem — that TWFE is a weighted average of 2×2 DiDs, some receiving negative weights when later-cohort treatment effects differ from early-cohort effects
expectations.evidence: Section 3 is titled 'The Goodman-Bacon decomposition: your specific exposure' and states: 'Goodman-Bacon (2021) proves that the TWFE coefficient is a weighted average of all possible 2×2 DiD estimators. The weights are determined by group sizes and the variance in treatment timing — not by which comparisons are cleanest.' Section 2 also notes: 'In extreme cases of treatment effect heterogeneity, TWFE can return a negative coefficient even when every cohort's true treatment effect is positive, because some implicit 2×2 DiD comparisons receive negative weight.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a heterogeneity-robust DiD estimator (e.g., Callaway-Sant'Anna, Sun-Abraham, or Borusyak-Jaravel-Spiess) rather than standard TWFE
expectations.evidence: Section 5 ('What to do instead') recommends Callaway & Sant'Anna (2021) as the primary estimator ('recommended for your case'), and also describes Sun & Abraham (2021) and de Chaisemartin & D'Haultfoeuille (2020) as alternatives. The summary table states: 'Is there a better approach? Yes. Callaway-Sant'Anna or Sun-Abraham, plus an event-study plot.'
